grammar_notes.title: Talking About the Past ('dzakasiyana')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'dzakasiyana' expresses a completed past action. Shona has two main ways to talk about the past: 1) For actions that happened earlier today or very recently, combine the short subject prefix ('nda-' = I, 'wa-' = you, 'a-' = he/she, 'ta-' = we, 'va-' = they) directly with the verb stem (e.g., 'ndamuka' = 'I woke up today', 'wabudirira' = 'you have succeeded'). 2) For events that happened yesterday or further in the past, insert '-ka-' after the subject prefix (e.g., 'takatenga' = 'we bought', 'vakaenda' = 'they went', 'akadanidzira' = 'he shouted').
grammar_notes.rule: Recent Today Past: [nda- / wa- / ta- / va-] + verb | Earlier Past: [ndaka- / waka- / taka- / vaka-] + verb

grammar_notes.title: Actions Happening Right Now: The '-ri ku-' Progressive
grammar_notes.content: To describe an action that is happening right now ('I am doing', 'it is raining', 'they are walking'), Shona uses the helper verb '-ri' ('am/is/are') followed by 'ku-' ('to') and the action verb. For people, the forms are 'ndiri ku-' (I am), 'uri ku-' (you are), 'ari ku-' (he/she is), 'tiri ku-' (we are), and 'vari ku-' (they are). In fast speech or writing, the two words are sometimes joined together (e.g., 'ndiri kuenda' or 'ndirikuenda').
grammar_notes.rule: [Subject + -ri] + ku-[verb] -> Ndiri kuverenga (I am reading) | Vari kufamba (They are walking) | Mvura iri kunaya (It is raining)

grammar_notes.title: Present Tense & Everyday Actions ('unonzi')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'unonzi' uses the present marker '-no-'. In Shona, inserting '-no-' between the subject prefix and the verb stem expresses general truths, everyday habits, or states of mind like 'wanting', 'thinking', and 'knowing'. For example: 'ndinoda' ('I want/like'), 'unofunga' ('you think'), 'vanoti' ('they say'), and 'vanorima' ('they farm').
grammar_notes.rule: [ndi- (I) / u- (you) / a- (he/she) / ti- (we) / va- (they)] + -no- + verb -> Ndinoda (I want), Vanogara (They live)

cultural_notes.title: Shona Cultural & Everyday Context (Lesson 1)
cultural_notes.content: This expression ('Vanhu pamwechete nemotokari zvirikufamba panosangana mugwagwa unonzi Semu Mujoma naRobhati Mugabe. Pane varume pamwechete nevakadzi varikumhanyidzana vachienda kunzvimbo dzakasiyana.' — "People on / at mwechete and / with motokari they are famba on / at nosangana in / singular gwagwa you nzi semu in / singular joma narobhati in / singular gabe on / at ne men on / at mwechete and / with vakadzi they are mhanyidzana people chienda to / at nzvimbo.") reflects how Shona speakers connect daily family life, work, and community relationships across urban towns and rural homesteads ('kumusha') in Zimbabwe.

active_exercises.prompt: Complete this sentence about travelling: 'Mangwana ______ bhazi rinoenda kuMasvingo.' (Tomorrow we will board the bus going to Masvingo.)
Translate this new sentence into English: 'Kombi chena iri kufamba pamugwagwa mukuru.'
options: The white minibus is travelling along the main road.
The large red truck is parked at the fuel station.
Two people are standing beside the shop in town.
Our journey to the mountains was long but enjoyable.
active_exercises.correct_answer: The white minibus is travelling along the main road.
active_exercises.explanation: 'Kombi chena' = 'The white minibus', 'iri kufamba' = 'is travelling', 'pamugwagwa mukuru' = 'along the main road'.

active_exercises.prompt: Your friend just passed her driving test! What do you say to congratulate her in Shona?
active_exercises.explanation: 'Makorokoto!' means 'Congratulations!' and 'nekubudirira kwako' means 'on your success'.
